scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The South Galway Set hails from the Gort area of Galway, Ireland.
It represents a regional variation of Irish set dancing, which evolved from French quadrilles brought to Ireland in the 18th and 19th centuries.
The set was popularized in the modern era by Connie Ryan and has been documented in several key publications since the late 20th century, including works by Terry Moylan (1985) and Pat Murphy (1995).
on_screen: Map: Ireland · Europe
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: As a social set dance, it is performed at céilís, set dancing workshops, and traditional music festivals.
It serves as a form of communal recreation and a means of preserving the specific regional dance identity of South Galway.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed in a square set of four couples.
Gents stand on the left of their partners.
The 1st Top Couple starts with their backs to the band.
Watch for Up jig step, Advance and Retire.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Square set; 1st Tops back to band, 2nd Tops opposite, 1st Sides to the left of 1st Tops.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The set is danced to two primary musical forms: reels and jigs.
Figures 1, 2, 3, and 5 are reels, while Figure 4 is a jig.
Listen for the Fiddle, Button Accordion, Concertina, Uilleann Pipes.
The pulse is 4/4 and 6/8 at about 115 beats a minute.

The music consists of driving Irish reels and jigs. The reels provide a steady 4/4 pulse for four of the five figures, while the fourth figure shifts to a 6/8 jig rhythm. The sound is characterized by the melodic interplay of traditional Irish instruments over a consistent tempo suitable for set dancing.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: In modern practice, the dance is performed in casual or semi-formal attire suitable for social dancing.
Historically, it would be danced in community halls or homes.
The setting requires enough space for a four-couple square to expand and contract during advance and retire movements.

Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Connie Ryan is a central figure in the preservation of this set, having included it in his instructional video series.
Other significant documentarians include Terry Moylan, Pat Murphy, Tom Quinn, and Joe O'Hara, who provided online versions for both workshop and traditional half-set formats.
Joe O'Hara identifies two main versions: a 4-couple workshop version and a traditional half-set version.
The South Galway Set belongs to the broader family of Irish set dances.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: South Galway Set is sibling of Clare Lancers Set: Both are Irish set dances with similar square formations, but South Galway uses a flatter step.
